title: Stranded in Oklahoma City and Guthrie under Mr. Brown
summary: A chaperoned tour pays 25 cents a man in Guthrie, and the boys survive on cabbages and watermelons taken from fields.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Well Budd, I just want to get back to this, then. When did you first -- now you, this is about 1927, and you all got the Blue Moon Chasers, not when did you get up to around Kansas City? When did you get out of Texas? When is the first time you guys, like when either you and Keg went on your own?
Okay, that's a little story before this, and this is leading up to what you asked me.
In 19 and 27 we got a call from a guy by the name of Eugene Coy, that is my brother and myself got this call, after we were back from one of these --

Okay, could I just say -- the reason when I'm saying we were back, we had gone out on a tour once more to Oklahoma City, and we got stranded again there. These were the stranded years. These were when you were paying your dues. And we went into Oklahoma City, and well then a man by the name of Mr. Brown, who was going to chaperone us, and our parents let us go away with, and we -- our first job out of Oklahoma City was in Guthrie, Oklahoma, which is now the capital of Oklahoma City, and -- of Oklahoma, I mean, and on the way to Guthrie, I

don't know, I imagine it's about 40, 45 miles from Oklahoma City. We -- in traveling there we were admiring the beautiful farms, and the big beautiful head of cabbages, and the watermelon patches, and the cantaloupes, and all the things, and the corn, and whatnot, beautiful farms.

So anyway, we went into Guthrie and we played this dance, so the hall was packed, and we were really good. I mean we were really good at that time, and the people loved it, and they'd dance, and they'd dance, and they'd dance. After the dance we got together and we went to Mr. Brown to be paid, and Mr. Brown said, "You know one thing," he said, "I don't know how all these people got in here. I had the police on the back door. I had the police on the front door. And whatnot." he said, but "they slipped in somehow."
Anyway, we did salvage 25 cents a man. And --
That's $25.00 you say, 25cents is a lot of --
I could do an awful lot with 25 cents in those days.
Two bits. A fourth part of a dollar.

And so now we knew we were in trouble, because we had gotten two rooms that a woman let us have upstairs. I forget her name, and I should never forget her name. She was very kind. And one was on a sleeping porch, a screened in sleeping porch upstairs, with cots, and the other was with one bedroom, and on the way back we decided we've got to eat, so we said hey, remember those beautiful cabbage patches we saw on the way, and it was dark, so said, Stop the car. So we stopped the car and slipped under the barb wire fence, and we pulled up cabbages and watermelons and cantaloupes, and we came back and the next morning when we woke up we had all of this stuff. We brought it up and the lady said, okay, you guys, you got to eat, so she said well look, you've got all this cabbage, and everything, so she says well I just bought a new washtub, one of those little small washtubs. She said, so you can cook it in there. So we put the -- cleaned the cabbage and everything, and we put it in the washtubs, and we took a few pennies of our money and went out and got some fatback -- you know what fatback is, don't you?

That's a streak of lean, and streak of pork, salted down, kind of, yeah. So we put that in there and we cooked this cabbage. And we all ate very heartily. We were full and feeling good, and so Mr. Brown, we didn't do any other work
